text: At first Bartleby did an extraordinary quantity of writing, as if long famishing for something to copy, but he worked on silently, palely, and mechanically, without a trace of cheerful industry. <break time="0.8s" /> On the third day, when I called him to examine a short paper with me, he replied, in a singularly mild, firm voice, I would prefer not to. <break time="0.8s" /> Had there been the least uneasiness, anger, or impertinence in his manner, I would have dismissed him at once, but his face was leanly composed and his gray eye dimly calm. <break time="0.8s" /> A few days later, when the four copies of a long document were ready to be examined, I called all my clerks together, but Bartleby, appearing at the entrance of his hermitage, calmly preferred not to join us. <break time="0.8s" /> When I demanded his reasons, he merely repeated, I would prefer not to, and, as often happens to a man resisted in some unprecedented way, I began to stagger in my own plainest faith. <break time="0.8s" /> Turning to my other clerks for support, I asked their opinion, whereupon Turkey declared, in his mild morning voice, that I was quite right, and Nippers proposed to kick the scrivener out of the office. <break time="0.8s" /> Nothing so aggravates an earnest person as passive resistance, yet, because Bartleby seemed to mean no harm, I resolved to construe his strange conduct charitably rather than to punish it. <break time="0.8s" /> To befriend him, I reasoned, would cost me little or nothing, while it would lay up in my soul what would eventually prove a sweet morsel for my conscience.
